label: The fitness function is not explicitly specified, making implementation and verification of the optimization objective difficult.
The proposed implications lack demonstrated applications and actionable guidance, including how the hypothesis improves theoretical understanding of neural networks.
Blind hashing may be inadequate for more complicated environments, which may require learned representations for density estimation.
Domain adaptation experiments appear to use test-set label marginals, giving the proposed method additional information unavailable to VADA.
The paper does not establish that its methodology improves upon existing methods.
Tables 1 and 2 lack side-by-side ablations assessing the utility of weight sharing and gating operations.
The phrase about changing transition probabilities contains an extraneous space before a comma.
Learning one graph per time period may miss short-term dependencies; an ablation should examine this limitation.
The experiments do not isolate whether BatchNorm's standardization improves the performance achievable by its affine transformation.
The reason Eq. (2) is non-negative is insufficiently explained.
The definition of “structures” is unclear, making Section 4 difficult to follow and its explanation of entity-marker behavior unconvincing.
Experiments test only one value of λ, without evaluating sensitivity to this hyperparameter controlling inverse rewards' influence.
Evaluation beyond the current dataset is needed to demonstrate the proposed approach's generalizability.
Comparisons use only very old approaches, leaving the state-of-the-art claim unsupported.
Figure 3 would be more informative with a logarithmic x-axis.
The paper does not test whether the findings hold with disjoint datasets or varying amounts of training data.
Theorem 2's iteration complexity grows with network width m, unlike Cai et al. (2019); this potentially loose dependence needs explanation or numerical justification.
The paper lacks a related-work section.
Interpreting Figures 3–4 appears to require external context, and the displayed results reveal only general trends.
Some figures in Section 3.4.2 are too small, with nearly unreadable labels.
The paper is densely written, omits technical details, and lacks sufficient explanations, context, and motivating examples for a broader audience.
The proposed approach is insufficiently studied empirically.
Figure 3 sometimes shows baseline performance very close to the proposed method.
Page 2 contains grammatical errors: 'relative recent' should be 'relatively recent,' and 'be applied directly learn' needs 'to.'
Section 2.1 does not clarify whether its five transformations exhaust relevant transformations or capture reward-function sets induced by objects such as expert demonstrations.
It is unclear whether the model uses generative training, such as variational approximate posterior inference, and how it could support generation otherwise.
Appendix A's proof of Theorem 1 is incomplete.
The empirical gains may be too small or uncertain to justify the algorithmic contributions' added complexity.
The paper lacks theoretical or empirical analysis of learning dynamics, such as current- and next-state value changes with and without the constraint.
Section 5.2 uses 'mean field' unconventionally for the decoder; 'conditionally independent' would be clearer.
Figure 8's caption inadequately explains the plots, particularly what the vertical axis reports.
Algorithm 2's random gradient scaling and task sampling lack justification compared with simply normalizing and summing task gradients.
Comparisons with simple, straightforward baseline methods are missing.
The paper does not justify why normalization-free networks should mimic ResNet's SPP trends.
The paper omits analysis of Hazan et al. (2015), which proposed Stochastic Normalized Gradient Descent (SNGD).
Experiments cover only MNIST, which is too easy for conclusive results; validation on ImageNet, CIFAR-100, or NLP datasets is needed.
Figure 1's restrictive setting inadequately supports the L_2-growth claim; CIFAR-10 experiments without batch normalization are needed to isolate dynamic ensemble behavior.
The paper lacks clear novel conceptual insights beyond prior information-maximization work such as Bell & Sejnowski (1995).
Technical novelty is limited: contrastive learning for Siamese Transformers and pseudo query-document pairs have already been studied, including in ICT.
All tasks use a simple 2-layer MLP baseline; it is unclear whether gains persist with more complex baseline models.
Related work omits discussion of Mott et al. 2019, Greydanus et al. 2018, and Yuezhang et al. 2018.
The benefit of restricting novel vectors to the base-class subspace is insufficiently explained, particularly given contrary motivation in Continual Learning in Low-rank Orthogonal Subspaces.
Table 2 uses a weak ImageNet-C baseline and omits stronger comparisons with AugMix and other publicly available methods.
Figure 2 lacks a clear interpretation.
The details in Appendix B should be included in the main paper.
It is unclear whether lambda in Eq. 2 is the same parameter as lambda in Eq. 6.
The authors do not compare identical architectures with and without scattering first layers, complicating attribution of performance differences.
The rebuttal appears to misidentify Mnih et al.'s Figure S9 as Figure 9.
The representation analysis offers insufficient insight beyond visual category grouping and deeper networks outperforming shallower networks in Figure 2.
Lemma 1's curvature results need clarification for mixed spherical, Euclidean, and hyperbolic products, including whether negative curvature contributions are ignored.
Section 3.4 does not justify parallel concept subspaces for hierarchical classification; the toucan–Dalmatian versus bird–dog example does not establish the claimed relationship.
Section 5.2's two reasons are jointly unconvincing; correlations should be reported both with and without averaging human scores.
None of the contributions are especially novel.
The proposed method's claimed optimization advantage over Adam or Amsgrad lacks justification.
The paper is not clearly written.
The computational cost of constructing M in each iteration is not quantified.
The experiments lack an ImageNet comparison.
Page 5's 'scaling the changes' should read 'scales the changes'.
The paper lacks accessible comparisons with published baseline values and explanations of discrepancies, making baseline implementation correctness difficult to assess.
Comparisons with InfoGAN and VEEGAN augmented with similar z reconstruction loss terms are missing.
Comparative results against PPO are missing.
The proposal is incremental, largely applying existing methods through a pipeline combining two previous papers.
Section 4.1.2 claims competitiveness with Yu, Chen, Lin, and Bilinski & Prisacariu, but their results are absent from the referenced figures.
Section 2.3 uses p without properly defining it; its only earlier appearance is in Equation 6.
A baseline combining the proposed data augmentation with label smoothing is missing.
The paper does not establish whether the proposed approach suffers from ACGAN-like within-class mode collapse favoring images whose y is easy to infer.
Unrolling sparse coding inference as a feed-forward network is not new.
Section 3.2 does not establish why ResNet-50's initially high squared weight norm demonstrates a drawback of rounding-to-nearest-even.
Equation (4) leaves i and j ranges and q_i^j dimensions unclear, including their correspondence to n_pc, pc_size, and pc_hidden in the appendix.
The method is not compared with Kurth-Nelson & Redish (2009) on Pathworld or Atari 2600, leaving the extensions' usefulness insufficiently demonstrated.
OE appears better than FROB on average, and guidelines for choosing FROB over OE are missing.
Equation 6 appears to be missing a minus sign.
The Mikolov citation in the abstract is incorrectly formatted.
Table 1's low accuracies call into question whether its performance comparisons are meaningful.
Page 2, paragraph 1 misuses “Moreover”: extreme weights arise from small Pr(t|x), and the resulting numerical instability causes high-variance estimates.
The choices of hyperparameters alpha, especially rho, appear ad hoc and need justification.
Section 6 evaluates density estimation but omits point-count estimation performance needed to support claims of new Poisson process modeling.
Section 7 lacks an explicit definition of delta-hyperbolicity.
The paper does not explain why the additional variant performs worse than the proposed approach.
The experiments lack comparison with semantics-based embedding techniques from Reed & De Freitas (2015).
Theorem 1's proof is inadequately justified, particularly the applicability of the Lipschitz assumptions from Nesterov et al.
The paper does not compare its solution and results against Deng et al. (2010, 2014) or HD-CNN.
In Lemma 3, an i should be x.
The log-concavity assumption appears to restrict the method to simpler models without learned representations, raising concerns about its suitability for ICLR.
The paper lacks side-by-side visual comparisons with other approaches.
Section 3.2.2 needs clarification.
The distinction between Theorem 7.2 and Corollary 5.3, and the claimed refinement rather than mere application, is unclear.
The explanation of Table 3 is confusing.
Section 4.2 essentially presents its second experiment only through a still image, without adequate textual description.
CIFAR10 error of 40% is worse than some simple fully connected models, raising concerns about training quality and meaningfulness.
The full-precision weight-update statement above Figure 1 appears inconsistent with Table 3's 8-bit gradient specification.
Performance improvements over the chosen baselines are only marginal.
Section 4.1's arguments need formal justification and a clearer statement of their intended conclusion about nonlinear activation.
CPN's distinction from momentum needs clarification through a conceptual saddle-point diagram or comparison with an R_t(f) yielding exact momentum updates.
The paper does not justify why the evaluation metric used in Table 1 is appropriate.
Figure 1 appears to reference Sections 3 and 4 incorrectly.
Theorem 2's proof does not clearly define T and t or specify which weights the expectation averages over, obscuring the recursion.
Section 3.1 is difficult to follow.
The phrase 'agent explores greedily wrt to Q function' misleadingly suggests a separate exploration phase; 'acts greedily' would be clearer.
Sec 2.4 lacks a final period.
The last paragraph of page 7 contains a duplicated 'with'.
The introduction repeatedly uses 'neural implicit' before defining it near the first inset.
Major experimental results appear only in Table 4 of Appendix D; at least selected results should appear in the main paper.
Experiments are limited to CelebA, providing insufficient dataset coverage.
Experiments are limited to a toy problem.
The choices of the two introduced hyperparameters and the hyperparameter tuning and model selection process are not explained.
Page 15, Theorem 1's proof does not clearly identify the matrices used to apply Lemma 8 or explain the sqrt(2) factor.
Ablations are missing, particularly comparisons using alternative unsupervised approaches.
Eq. (2) does not explain what i and j denote.
Table 2 shows only marginal improvement over the existing method.
Experiments should evaluate different basis choices more thoroughly.
The paper contains many typos.
Privacy guarantees for sharing extracted knowledge reflecting differences between local models are insufficiently discussed.
The proposed algorithms lack theoretical guarantees, such as an upper bound on $|\rho^* - \hat{\rho}^*|$ establishing convergence.
Statistical significance tests, such as t-tests, are missing for the proposed approach's improvements over baselines.
The paper needs proofreading.
Algorithm 1, line 5, should explicitly reference Equation 5.
Sparse residuals, apparently the core departure from prior techniques, need greater emphasis and explanation in the introduction.
Theorem 1 is trivial because its assumption equates numerical and true directional derivatives; orthogonalizing and normalizing k+P random normal vectors also satisfies it.
Section 1 lacks sufficient theoretical analysis supporting the conjecture that an adequate weight matrix spectrum matters for GAN training.
The figures lack error bars.
It is unclear whether the reported baselines are sufficiently close to state of the art to support meaningful comparisons.
The work's novelty over existing methods is not significant.
Section 4.3 does not clearly define how Mean Concept AUC is calculated.
Architecture details, including component layers, CNN structure, nonlinearities, and dimensionalities, are incomplete or inconsistently provided.
The data representation is unclear and inconsistent: pixels are described as both request counts and presence/absence indicators.
The main results and intuition are obscured by details that could be moved to appendices.
The paper offers no clear intuition for why the proposed approach should be effective.
The method offers limited novelty over the authors' Wang et al. KDD work, mainly replacing some latent factors with RNNs.
Evaluating on D4RL is insufficiently justified given the argument that it does not represent the intended real-world resource-constrained setting.
Real numbers should be denoted by \mathbb{R}, not \mathcal{R}.
No clear explanation or evaluation establishes why fractional routing is more efficient than the original non-trainable CapsuleNet routing.
The paper's contributions are not clearly explained.
The claim that the algorithms yield significantly improved training across varied settings lacks sufficient empirical support.
The contribution appears small given the assumption of access to many MDPs with different reward densities, which makes the approach's effectiveness unsurprising.
Experiments lack comparisons with recent model-based RL methods.
The approach has limited novelty from a machine-learning standpoint.
The claimed suitability for high-dimensional data lacks sufficient analytical results concerning dimensionality.
Related-work coverage is inadequate, notably omitting Cai et al.'s ICLR 2017 paper.
Experimental results show no remarkable advantage over existing approaches.
The paper lacks intuition about how restrictive Assumptions 1 and 2 are.
Table 1 lacks results for CoE-Small/Large without knowledge distillation, preventing assessment of its contribution.
The proposed losses may require careful weight tuning, leaving unclear whether improvements reflect the losses themselves or favorable tuning.
The method's limitation to fixed-length sequences should be acknowledged and discussed.
Page 4 misspells 'structure' as 'stracture'.
The method requires manually derived generalized coordinates and forward/inverse kinematics using known physics, rather than learning these transformations, limiting novelty and generality.
The experiments omit Dai et al. (2015)'s IMDB and Rotten Tomatoes sentiment analysis tasks as alternatives to machine translation evaluation.
The quantitative semantic similarity results are not convincing, although the reviewer expresses uncertainty due to limited familiarity with the literature.
Assumption 2's requirement that f(x_i, ·) have no critical points appears overly restrictive and potentially excludes quadratic loss.
The assumption that chosen masks separate useful features from distractors is unjustified; experts may not know which features a model will use.
Code is not provided, limiting reproducibility.
The classification-only scope is not clearly stated, especially in Section 3.
Figure 5 does not clarify whether its x-axis counts environment interactions or model retraining iterations, nor how these quantities relate.
The paper lacks discussion clarifying the O(k^r) bound's practical limitations or identifying scenarios where it yields useful generalization guarantees.
Experiments lack comparisons with state-of-the-art graph-based, model-assumption approaches, leaving relative molecular validity and variety unestablished.
The loss function in Equation 7 is inadequately explained.
The method's scalability and effectiveness with a large number of classification targets are not established.
Evaluation on only two Atari games is insufficient to establish general performance; results on more games or other domains are needed.
The paper lacks comparison with a simpler replacement rule using rare source-target words occurring in exactly the same sentence pairs.
Evaluation should include more widely used short-text classification datasets, such as TREC.
The paper insufficiently justifies its architectural choices.
Section 4.3.2 lacks a detailed analysis of the effect of each model layer.
The experiments lack non-toy datasets.
Despite the Neural GPU extensions, elaborate curriculum requirements leave its usefulness for practical problems unclear.
Table 1 uses opaque labels A, B, C, and D that are difficult to cross-reference instead of understandable shorthand.
Training time, computational cost, and memory cost are not reported or compared with the baseline method.
ABM is substantially more computationally expensive than matching networks, requiring 90% test-pixel and 80% reference-pixel embedding dropout for feasible training.
ND-Adam may effectively revert to SGD with harmful ±1 weight constraints; its Figure 1B learning rate of 0.05 resembles optimal SGD settings.
Algorithm 1 is unclear and needs rewriting.
There are no comparisons with existing methods, including representative baselines such as Pathak et al. (2017) and Bellemare et al. (2016).
Section 2's discussion of train-batch versus full-batch loss is unclear, especially since full-dataset evaluation is feasible on smaller datasets.
The experimental results are weak.
The necessity and feasibility of learning a "full classifier" and satisfying the overlapping-support condition are unclear, given neural networks' simplicity bias.
The experiments lack a baseline using distances between raw images, such as the L2 norm of image differences.
Section 4 should acknowledge unfair synthetic comparisons with plain classifier and autoencoder baselines, which cannot distinguish correct signals from distractors during training.
The equations use nonstandard notation, such as “softplus,” making them hard to read.
The experiments, including reruns, do not convincingly establish which regularization helps under which circumstances, why it helps, or when it fails.
Computing the new policy separately for each state appears to restrict the method to tabular policies, undermining the arbitrary-parameterization claim.
Related Work categorizes pruning techniques but does not discuss prior work in relation to effective sparsity.
The paper lacks an example or lower bound demonstrating a significant gap between its loss bounds and the best NTK or kernel-method bounds.
The experimental setup is incompletely defined, including which datasets are used for evaluation.
Proposition 4 uses "exits" instead of "exists".
The introduction's suggested link between adversarial examples and learning algorithms is tenuous.
The assertion that small networks are appropriate for the training data lacks supporting evidence.
Section 3.4 briefly provides only a loss function, leaving insufficient algorithmic detail for practitioners to implement the method.
The technical contribution is incremental and may lack sufficient novelty for ICLR.
The title of Section 3.3 contains a typo.
The paper provides no convergence analysis of the full stochastic algorithm.
Figure 1 omits the discriminator and real data, making the graphical summary incomplete.
The paper lacks an explanation for why different per-layer learning rates improve performance.
The Atari experiments omit applying the exploration technique to DQN despite comparisons against DQN-based methods.
The contributions and method need clearer exposition; pseudocode of the complete procedure would help.
Evaluation uses only tiny tasks; larger datasets and models, including language modeling on Wiki or LM1B and translation on English–German, are missing.
Experiment code, pre-training datasets, and pre-trained models should be released for reproducibility.
The experiments do not establish whether gains arise from the proposed model or its potentially larger parameter count.
The discussion insufficiently differentiates the framework from transfer learning approaches.
Q and P lack consistent interpretations and depart from standard VAE encoder and decoder notation.
The paper lacks strong theoretical support.
Experiments cover only the StarIntruders environment, providing insufficient evidence for the method's empirical improvements.
The paper lacks human evaluation of generative explanations on a subset of test data.
The method does not explain how it handles generators reconstructing nearly identical original images after many iterations, leaving little for the segmentation model to learn.
In-house dataset comparisons omit BERT QA top-k span-selection heuristics, such as diversity and overlap prevention, which could reduce the reported gap.
The work lacks sufficient novelty because character information and residual networks have already been used in prior work.
The experiments lack comparisons with more competitive baselines.
A human study is needed to establish that gains reflect caption quality rather than overfitting word-matching metrics through frequent COCO attributes.
Equation (9) does not specify the distributions of epsilon and gamma used in the expectation.
The paper lacks comparisons of computational complexity or execution time across methods.
Unexplained early-ending curves and potentially inconsistent x-axes for 4 or 16 gradient updates make apparent learning-speed improvements unreliable.
Section 2.3 (Learned embedding) is confusing and would benefit from clearer explanation, such as an algorithm block.
Method descriptions and analysis do not clearly explain how methodological differences produce the experimental results or what takeaways readers should draw.
Table 3 lacks sufficient investigation and explanation of why the experimental choices and groups yield their reported performance.
The proposed model performs worse than the baseline on the real-world dataset.
The paper lacks novelty and offers limited methodological contributions.
The recurrence definition r(s) should include i, for example r(s_i), to clarify the time-dependent subset of previous states and avoid an apparently undefined variable.
The paper does not justify why its decomposition of h is appropriate.
The many-component network appears difficult to train accurately and may require undisclosed practical training tricks.
The tradeoffs introduced by representation replay and how to choose them are unclear.
Figure 1b's dashed line is hard to read, and its colors are insufficiently distinguishable.
The paper's scope is too narrow for ICLR because its application is highly specific.
Figures 3 and 4 omit MLP.
The WaveNet implementation fails to outperform the baseline LSTM-RNN, making comparisons with WaveNet unconvincing.
Some references are confusing.
Even the revised five random seeds inadequately capture RL variance; at least 30 seeds were expected for reliable comparisons.
Evaluation is limited to smaller datasets; larger image datasets such as ImageNet-10 should be included.
The result has limited practical relevance because it describes an undesirable regime and excludes structured priors that benefit deep learning applications.
The experiments lack a Pathworld-like deep RL domain with trajectory-dependent increasing risk, high-dimensional states, and continuous actions to demonstrate effectiveness.
Task descriptions and Table 1 insufficiently explain the tasks, classes, and label meanings, leaving unclear what is tested.
Section 4.3 does not justify restricting the dataset to mRNA when the database also contains non-messenger RNA data and annotations.
The total number of training iterations used in experiments is unspecified.
Section 3.6 does not explain how many latent z variables to generate, making the variable-sized latent state exposition confusing.
The claimed aim of robustness agnostic to test-time noise is not established by improvements on only some corrupted datasets.
The practical benefit of introducing synchronization into asynchronous training is not evaluated.
For realistically large k, least-squares solves or gradient updates may dominate runtime rather than hard thresholding, limiting the proposed acceleration's practical benefit.
The reported lack of improvement from LSTM models may reflect insufficient training data for more complex models, making the comparison difficult to interpret.
Section 3.1 introduces heavy, confusing notation, including the unexplained superscript in s_t^{3-p}, which is inconsistently used afterward, including in Figure 1.
Full rotational equivariance may be less important in the mechanical domains discussed because gravity breaks symmetry along an axis.
The paper exceeds eight pages without clearly justifying the extra length.
The theoretical analysis provides no new insights.
The comparison lacks matching networks augmented with residual connections and dropout, which could isolate hypercolumn embedding benefits and close ABM's performance gap.
The Predictive Sample Selection method lacks concrete analysis.
Paper-title capitalization in the references needs correction.
Page 2's phrase 'that is universal approximator' is missing the article 'a'.
Page 7's VGG16 results sentence incorrectly includes CIFAR100 after 'SVHN and CIFAR10.'
Some citations use incorrect formats through inappropriate use of \cite and \citep.
The paper lacks detailed analysis of the approach's drawbacks relative to conventional generative models.
The evaluation lacks a stronger downstream task.
Sections 4.2–4.3 do not establish whether generated training and test sets were verified to be disjoint.
The references are incorrectly formatted.
The spelling "ImageNet-c" should be corrected to "ImageNet-C".
Experiments lack comparisons with recent state-of-the-art defenses, such as those listed at www.robust-ml.org/defenses/.
Related work omits Wang et al., 'Learning to model the tail' (NIPS 2017), relevant to weight generation or adaptive embeddings.
Weak link and node prediction performance does not adequately support the claim that the model generalizes.
Scalability to ImageNet is insufficiently discussed: temporal ensembling requires approximately 4.8 GB of storage, while Π-model doubles training time.
The choice of reward r = log(Discriminator) lacks justification and discussion of alternatives.
Riemannian TransE underperforms baselines on WN18 and FB15k, but those results are not reported.
Equations 4 and 5 use inconsistent notation.
Terminology about pre-training and methods lacking a training phase is unclear; KPCA's closed-form update still constitutes training.
The results lack error bars from multiple random seeds.
Definitions throughout the paper are unclear.
Related work inadequately covers recent multiagent deep RL, including papers by Foerster, Sukhbataar, and Omidshafiei.
Section 3.2 does not explain why Figure 6 demonstrates that Equation 5's second term has little effect.
The paper needs a gradient-boosting overview with formulas and Equation (3)'s derivation, explicitly connecting the proposed modifications to standard boosting.
All equations lack punctuation.
The performance gains do not sufficiently justify the increased training and inference costs; the cost-performance trade-off needs analysis.
Page 5 defines a bad-type neuron through B1 or B2, leaving the role of B3 unclear.
Equation (5) misleadingly subscripts alpha with k-1 even though it defines a function of alpha; the subscript should be removed.
On page 3, seventh line from bottom, f^{(2)}(x) incorrectly contains f_i^{(1)}(x) rather than f_i^{(2)}(x).
The claim that synthetic tokens are necessary for DNA/RNA ignores direct one-hot encoding used by DeepBind and DeepSea; k-mer tokenization is optional.
Reliable generalization from training responses c(r) to desired c(r*) remains uncharacterized; restricting c* to training support is insufficient, as Fig6d illustrates.
The proposed regularization methods are simple and already known.
The benefit of learned per-exemplar classification weights needs more ablation evidence; Table 3 provides only one experiment with marginal improvements.
Boldface is used excessively, and the occasional red font is unnecessary.
The claimed ability to generate trees in time proportional to tree depth is not empirically validated.
Table 4's DANN performance for S=6 and T=A is anomalous relative to other results and needs explanation.
The method's simple foreground-background composition may not handle complex real-world images with multiple compositional layers, limiting its generality.
The evaluation may mistake failure to optimize Eq. (12) for absence of attacks, making reported errors questionable when no successful attack is found.
Combining recurrent layers with CNNs offers limited novelty over Bell et al. (2016); cascading rather than parallel recurrence constitutes only a minor change.
The paper does not establish why quantization or uniform noise is preferable to directly adding noise, such as Gaussian noise.
The efficiency of training the neural encoder-decoder models lacks theoretical analysis.
Section 2.7's STDP comparison overlooks e_t's backpropagating-error role; applying the plotted spike-timing rule in an ordinary STDP setting would not implement error backpropagation.
Table 4 compares results across different settings; ORQA uses an open setting, whereas this paper apparently does not.
Code is not provided.
The tables omit exact parameter counts for each model despite reduced parameter count being central to the argument.
Evaluation is limited to two simple image datasets, two architectures, and classification, leaving generalization to text, speech, or regression untested.
The paper overlooks Faster RCNN, whose learned object proposals substantially outperform EdgeBoxes.
The statistical mechanism by which random walks capture higher-order subgraph features is unclear.
The abstract's phrase 'mixed with irrelevant ...' contains a typo or unclear wording and needs rewriting.
Significant apparent overlap with Cazenave 2016a leaves the paper's novelty unclear; the referenced paper could not be found.
Section 5.2 and Table 2 unfairly compare MDA using known test-time perturbations against ERM without equivalent data augmentation.
The emphasis on avoiding Hessian inversion is misleading: existing methods solve linear systems or differentiate backward without inverting Hessians, weakening Algorithm 2's motivation.
Algorithm pseudocode is missing, making practical implementation difficult to understand.
The phrase 'are not incompatible' should be simplified to 'are compatible'.
Comparisons with unstructured pruning, rather than only channel pruning, are missing.
Figure 4 sampling trajectories can enter regions without real samples; the method lacks a mechanism to detect and stop these trajectories.
Explicit regularization uses the Frobenius norm rather than the derived ||J1||², without justification or experiments regularizing the latter.
Table 1's NTM baseline has 31% error versus 20% in Graves et al. (2016), suggesting inadequate hyperparameter tuning.
The experiments provide insufficient evidence that the method generalizes beyond the evaluated settings.
The paper does not explain why ChebNet cannot work with unnormalized Laplacians while CayleyNet can.
Comparisons with H2 and H5 are unfair because different sampling strategies give the proposed method and baselines different training and testing sets.
Section 3.2 does not specify the comparison metric for the 300-dimensional real vectors, such as L2 distance or inner product.
